video.title: Did God Really FORSAKE Jesus on the Cross? What "Eli, Eli, Lama Sabachthani" Points To
video.description:
Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" When Jesus cried these words from the cross at the ninth hour, did God really turn His face away from His own Son, or is there something in this cry that most readers walk straight past?

In this Bible study we stand on that darkened hillside and look closely at the most famous sentence Jesus spoke from the cross, beginning with a question few people ask: why did the crowd standing right beside Him think He was calling for Elijah? You will see why Matthew writes Eli while Mark writes Eloi, why the word sabachthani is Aramaic rather than Hebrew, and how the Hebrew word behind it in Psalm 22, azav, is the very word God used when He promised never to forsake His people in Deuteronomy 31:6 and Psalm 37:25. We follow the strong Greek verb the Gospel writers chose for the cry and find it again in one of the most loved promises in the New Testament, Hebrews 13:5, "I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee." Then we look at how people in the first century often pointed to a passage by its opening words, and we lay Psalm 22 line by line beside the crucifixion: the darkness at noon, the mockers wagging their heads, the words "He trusted in God; let him deliver him," the thirst, and the soldiers casting lots for His garments, which John connects to the psalm outright. We also look honestly at the debated line about pierced hands and feet and what the Septuagint and the traditional Hebrew text each say. From there we follow the sudden turn in the psalm, "thou hast heard me," the promise to declare God's name to "my brethren," and the risen Jesus sending word to His brethren about "my God, and your God." We place the psalm's vision of the nations turning to the Lord next to the Roman centurion who stood facing the cross, consider two respectful ways Christians have understood this cry, and close with Luke's "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit" and John's "It is finished." If you have ever felt that God walked away from you, this study shows that the most faithful man who ever lived brought his darkest question to the God he still called "my God."

Which line of Psalm 22 speaks to you most today? Share it in the comments, even a single verse, and subscribe so you do not miss the next study as we keep reading the Scriptures slowly and together. God bless you.

Sources mentioned:
The Septuagint
The King James Version
The traditional Hebrew text of the Psalms

transcript.text: It is the ninth hour.
For 3 hours, darkness has lain over all the land.
A man hangs on a Roman cross.
A centurion stands facing him, watching.
Then the man cries out with a loud voice.
Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?
My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
You know this moment.
So here is the question almost nobody asks out loud.
Did God really abandon his own son on that cross?
Many of us were taught that he did.
The father turned his face away.
Heaven went silent.
The son was left completely alone in the dark.
And if you have ever sat somewhere in your own life and wondered whether God had simply walked out, that cry can feel very close to home.
But there is something in this moment most readers walk straight past.
Jesus did not invent these words.
They had been written down centuries earlier.
They are the opening line of Psalm 22, a psalm that carries the heading A Psalm of David.
Eli simply means my God.
If Jesus is quoting a psalm the whole nation knew, why did the people standing right beside him not recognize it?
Matthew tells us they heard something else entirely.
Matthew 27:47 says...

I will not azav you.
And now, at the ninth hour, the son of God takes that exact word and turns it into a question.
Why have you done the one thing you promised never to do?
Sit with that.
Whatever this crime means, it is not soft.
The word is real.
The darkness is real.
The question is real.
We are not going to make it smaller than the text makes it.
When the gospel writers carried the cry into Greek, they chose a strong word as well.
The Greek verb is enkaleipo.
It means to leave someone behind, to leave them in the lurch, to desert them when they needed you.
And then that very same Greek verb appears in one of the best loved promises in the New Testament.
Hebrews chapter 13, verse 5.
For he hath said, I will never leave thee nor forsake thee.
Nor forsake thee, enkaleipo.
The very word from the cross.
Keep that verse close.
It will matter before we are done.
So the question stands at full weight.
If the word is that strong, why does it matter that Jesus is quoting a Psalm at all?
To see that, you need to know how people in the first century carried their scriptures around.
There were no chapter and verse numbers.
Those came more than a thousand years later.
So people very often pointed to a passage by naming a phrase from it, especially its opening words.

transcript.text: My strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws.
John chapter 19 verse 28, After this, Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, saith, I thirst.
Then verse 16 of the Psalm, For dogs have compassed me, the assembly of the wicked have enclosed me.
They pierced my hands and my feet.
This line is debated.
The traditional Hebrew text reads something closer to, like a lion, my hands and my feet.
The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before the time of Jesus, reads, they pierced.
And the King James follows it.
I would not build anything on this one line alone.
And then verse 18,
They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.
On this verse, we do not need to guess what the Gospel writers were thinking.
John tells us outright.
John chapter 19, verse 23 and 24.
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part.
And also his coat.
Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.
They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be.
That the scripture might be fulfilled, which saith, They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots.
That the scripture might be fulfilled.
John names Psalm 22 in the middle of the crucifixion itself.
This is not one stray verse borrowed for a dramatic moment.
The Psalm is being lived out around him, line by line, while he prays its first words.
If this is opening something up for you that you have not seen before, take a second and share it with someone who loves digging into the text like this.
Now come back to the cross.
Because if Psalm 22 only described suffering, it would explain the scene, but it would not answer the question.
Did God really forsake him?
To answer that, you have to do what that crowd did not do.
You have to keep listening.
Because Psalm 22 does not end where it begins.
Verse 19.
But be not thou far from me, O Lord.
O my strength, haste thee to help me.
Verse 20.
Deliver my soul from the sword, my darling from the power of the dog.
My darling, in the English of the King James, does not mean a loved one.
It means my only life, the one precious thing I have left.
Verse 21.
Save me from the lion's mouth, for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns.
Did you catch it?
In the middle of that verse, something turns.
The first half is a plea, Save me.
The second half is a statement, Thou hast heard me.
The unicorns, in the King James, are most likely wild oxen.
But do not miss the turn.
In Hebrew, thou hast heard me is a single word, anitani, you have answered me.
This is where the whole Psalm turns.
20 verses of crying out.
Then, in the middle of a sentence, the answer arrives.
The same man who said in verse 2, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not,
now says, you have answered me.
The Psalm does not explain how, it simply turns.
And from that moment, the whole Psalm changes its voice.
Verse 22.
I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee.
The man who was alone on the hill is suddenly standing in a crowd.
Not a crowd of mockers, a congregation, his brothers, and he is singing.
The New Testament does something remarkable with this verse.
The writer of Hebrews takes it and places it in the mouth of Jesus.

transcript.text: My God, and your God.
Three days earlier, in the dark, he cried, My God, my God.
Now, in the morning, he says it again, My God.
And then, he adds two words he had never said in quite this way before.
Your God.
The prayer that began in abandonment ends in a family.
There is one more verse in the middle of this psalm that speaks straight to our question.
Psalm 22 verse 24.
He hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted.
Neither hath he hid his face from him, but when he cried unto him, he heard.
Read it again slowly.
Neither hath he hid his face from him, but when he cried unto him, he heard.
This is the same psalm that begins, Why hast thou forsaken me?
And within the psalm itself, the question is answered.
God did not despise the one who suffered.
God did not hide his face.
When he cried, God heard.
But we have not finished with the hillside.
Do you remember the Centurion?
The soldier standing facing the cross in the very first seconds of this study?
Psalm 22 does not stop with the brothers.
It keeps widening like a ripple in water.
Verse 27.
All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the Lord, and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee.
All the kindreds of the nations, not only Israel, the Gentiles, the ends of the earth.
Now go back to Mark chapter 15.
The cry has been heard, and heard.
The sponge has been lifted on the reed.
Jesus cries out one last time and breathes his last.
And then, verse 39.
And when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw that he so cried out and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly, this man was the Son of God.
That means he stood directly facing him.
He had been watching the whole time.
Notice what Mark puts in front of us.
The crowd who knew the psalm heard a man calling for Elijah.
The Roman soldier, who very likely had never heard Psalm 22 in his life, watched the way this man died and confessed the Son of God.
In Mark's gospel, the first human being to look at the crucified Jesus and call him the Son of God is a Gentile, an officer of Rome, one of the kindreds of the nations turning.
It is hard not to hear the closing lines of Psalm 22 in that moment.
The man who stood there in the dark at the opening of our story, silently watching, may be the first answer to the end of the psalm.
The cry began, why hast thou forsaken me?
And the first voice from the watching nations to answer it is the one nobody would have expected.
So where does all this leave our question?
Did God really forsake Jesus on the cross?
Christians have understood this moment in more than one way, and both deserve to be heard with care.
Many believers, across many traditions, understand that on the cross Jesus truly bore the weight of sin and entered into the separation it brings.
They point to 2 Corinthians chapter 5 verse 21.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
And to Galatians chapter 3 verse 13.
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.
On this reading, the cry tells us that what Jesus carried was not pretend.
He went into the darkest place a human soul can go so that those who belong to him would never have to go there alone.
Other believers, also across many traditions, emphasize that the father and the son were never truly torn apart.
They point to the psalm itself.
He hath not hid his face from him.
And they point to something Jesus said on the night before he died.
John chapter 16 verse 32.
Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone.
And yet, I am not alone, because the father is with me.
These two readings are not as far apart as they may sound.
Psalm 22 holds both of them in one song.
It begins in a genuine experience of abandonment.
The man in the psalm is not acting.
He feels forsaken, and he says so.
And the same psalm ends with the testimony that God did not hide his face, that the cry was heard, that the afflicted one was not despised.
You do not have to choose between the darkness and the answer.
The psalm puts them side by side, and Jesus prays the first line of that psalm.
